title: NSAIDs and Alcohol: Ibuprofen, Naproxen, Aspirin and Rx Risks
excerpt: Can you mix NSAIDs and alcohol? How ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, and prescription NSAIDs interact with drinking, how they compare, how long to wait, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you mix NSAIDs and alcohol? How ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, and Rx NSAIDs affect your stomach and kidneys when you drink, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most healthy adults, one standard dose of an NSAID (ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin) the morning after a few drinks, taken with food and water, is unlikely to cause harm. The real risks come from three places: your stomach lining, your kidneys, and your blood's ability to clot. Alcohol pushes on all three, and NSAIDs push on the same three. The danger goes up with higher doses, several days in a row, an empty stomach, dehydration, and drinking 3 or more drinks a day. This guide explains how the whole drug family interacts with alcohol, how the common ones compare, where prescription NSAIDs fit in, and the warning signs that mean you should get help.

**The quick rules:** Don't take an NSAID before bed "to head off" a hangover. If you drink 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor or pharmacist before using any NSAID. If you take one after a night out, take a single label dose with food and a full glass of water, and don't stack two different NSAIDs. If you take a prescription NSAID every day, ask your prescriber how much alcohol, if any, is reasonable for you.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining NSAIDs and alcohol if** you have had a stomach ulcer or stomach bleeding, have kidney disease, heart disease, or high blood pressure, take a blood thinner, a steroid, an SSRI antidepressant, or blood pressure medicine, are over 60, or drink 3 or more drinks most days. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, pass black or tarry stools, have severe stomach pain, or feel faint or dizzy after taking an NSAID while drinking.

## What Counts as an NSAID?

NSAID stands for **non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug**. It's a family of medicines that reduce pain, fever, and inflammation. They all work the same basic way, so they share the same basic alcohol problem. The differences between them are mostly about how strong they are and how long they stay in your body.

**Over-the-counter NSAIDs in the US:**

- **Ibuprofen** (Advil, Motrin, store brands)
- **Naproxen sodium** (Aleve, store brands)
- **Aspirin** (Bayer, Ecotrin, and inside combination products like Excedrin and Alka-Seltzer)

**Common prescription NSAIDs:**

- **Meloxicam** (Mobic)
- **Diclofenac** (Voltaren, Cataflam, Arthrotec)
- **Celecoxib** (Celebrex)
- **Indomethacin**, **etodolac**, **nabumetone**, and **ketorolac**
- **Prescription-strength ibuprofen and naproxen** (for example 600 mg or 800 mg ibuprofen tablets)

**Not an NSAID:** acetaminophen (Tylenol, called paracetamol outside North America). It's a pain and fever reliever, but it works differently and doesn't reduce inflammation in the same way. Its alcohol risk is mainly to the liver rather than the stomach, which is why it gets its own guide: [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

A lot of people don't realize how many products contain an NSAID. Cold and sinus pills (Advil Cold and Sinus, Aleve-D), "PM" versions (Advil PM, Aleve PM), menstrual pain products, and some headache and stomach remedies all include one. Look for ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin (sometimes listed as acetylsalicylic acid) in the Drug Facts box.

## How NSAIDs and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

NSAIDs work by blocking enzymes called **COX-1 and COX-2** (cyclooxygenase). These enzymes make prostaglandins, which are chemical messengers that trigger pain and swelling. Blocking them is how NSAIDs relieve a headache or a sore knee.

The trouble is that prostaglandins also do useful jobs elsewhere in the body. Three of those jobs matter a lot when you've been drinking.

### 1. Prostaglandins protect your stomach lining

Your stomach is full of strong acid. Prostaglandins help it protect itself by keeping up a layer of mucus and bicarbonate on the stomach wall and keeping blood flowing to the lining so it can repair itself. When an NSAID blocks prostaglandins (mainly through COX-1), that protective layer gets thinner.

Alcohol attacks the same lining from a different direction. It irritates the stomach wall directly and increases acid. It can cause inflammation of the stomach lining (gastritis) on its own, which is one reason [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) is so common.

Put the two together and you have a lining that's being irritated by alcohol while its defenses are turned down by the NSAID. That's why every over-the-counter NSAID label in the US carries a **stomach bleeding warning** that specifically mentions alcohol. Since the FDA's 2009 labeling rule, those labels say the chance of stomach bleeding is higher if you have **3 or more alcoholic drinks every day** while using the product, along with other risk factors like being over 60 or having had ulcers.

### 2. Prostaglandins keep blood flowing to your kidneys

When you're well hydrated, your kidneys don't lean on prostaglandins much. When you're dehydrated, they lean on them heavily, because prostaglandins widen the small blood vessels that feed the kidneys and keep filtering going.

Alcohol is a diuretic. It suppresses the hormone vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate more and end up behind on fluids. (Our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) goes into this.) Add vomiting or a sweaty night of dancing and you can be meaningfully dehydrated by morning.

That is exactly when an NSAID is hardest on the kidneys. With prostaglandins blocked and fluid low, blood flow to the kidneys can drop. In healthy young people taking a single dose, this rarely causes a real problem. In older adults, people with kidney disease, people with heart failure, or anyone who is badly dehydrated, NSAIDs can cause an acute kidney injury.

### 3. Some NSAIDs make it harder for your blood to clot

COX-1 in your platelets (the cell fragments that plug leaks in blood vessels) makes a substance called thromboxane that helps them stick together. NSAIDs reduce this, so bleeding takes longer to stop.

- **Aspirin** does this permanently. It disables COX-1 in each platelet for the rest of that platelet's life, which is roughly 7 to 10 days. That's why low-dose aspirin is used to prevent heart attacks, and why its bleeding effect outlasts the drug itself.
- **Ibuprofen and naproxen** do it temporarily. The effect fades as the drug leaves your body.

Heavy drinking can also affect platelets and clotting, particularly over time. So a bleed that starts in an irritated stomach can be harder to stop. This is also why NSAIDs plus alcohol plus a blood thinner is a particularly risky mix. If you take one, read our guide on [blood thinners and alcohol](/never-hungover/blood-thinners-and-alcohol) and speak to your prescriber before using any NSAID.

### What about the liver?

NSAIDs are generally much easier on the liver than high doses of acetaminophen, which is why people often reach for them after drinking. Liver injury from NSAIDs does happen, but it's uncommon, and diclofenac is the one most often linked to it in the medical literature. If you have liver disease, though, the picture changes. Advanced liver disease (especially cirrhosis) makes NSAIDs more likely to cause kidney problems and bleeding, and many doctors advise people with cirrhosis to avoid them. That's a conversation for your doctor, not a label.

### Does aspirin raise your blood alcohol?

Possibly a little. A small study published in *JAMA* in 1990 found that taking aspirin before drinking led to higher blood alcohol levels than drinking without it. The suggested reason is that aspirin reduces an alcohol-breaking enzyme in the stomach lining, so more alcohol reaches your bloodstream. Later studies have been mixed on how much this matters. It's not a big enough effect to plan around, but it's one more reason not to take aspirin before a night out.

## Ibuprofen vs Naproxen vs Aspirin With Alcohol: How They Compare

All three carry the same stomach bleeding warning. The main practical differences are how long they last, which matters if you're thinking about drinking later in the day.

| | Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) | Naproxen (Aleve) | Aspirin (Bayer, Excedrin) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Typical OTC adult dose | 200 to 400 mg every 4 to 6 hours | 220 mg every 8 to 12 hours | 325 to 650 mg every 4 hours |
| OTC daily limit on the label | 1,200 mg (6 tablets) unless a doctor says otherwise | 660 mg (3 tablets) in 24 hours | 4,000 mg (12 regular tablets) in 24 hours |
| How long it lasts in the body | Short (half-life about 2 hours) | Long (half-life roughly 12 to 17 hours) | Drug clears quickly, but the platelet effect lasts about a week |
| Stomach bleeding warning mentions alcohol | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Effect on clotting | Temporary | Temporary, but longer | Permanent for the life of each platelet |
| Main extra concern with alcohol | Kidneys when dehydrated | Lingers longer, so "wait time" is longer | Bleeding, and possible rise in blood alcohol |

A few things fall out of that table.

**Ibuprofen is the shortest-acting**, which makes it the most forgiving if you take one dose in the morning and might have a drink in the evening. Our [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) guide covers it in detail, and [Advil or Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) compares it head to head with acetaminophen.

**Naproxen lasts much longer.** One Aleve tablet can still be working 12 hours later. That's convenient for a sore back but means its stomach and kidney effects overlap with any drinking you do later the same day. See [Aleve and alcohol](/never-hungover/aleve-and-alcohol) for more.

**Aspirin's bleeding effect outlasts the pill.** Even a single aspirin affects clotting for days. If you take daily low-dose aspirin for your heart, don't stop it on your own because you plan to drink, and ask your doctor what's reasonable. Our [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) and [Excedrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/excedrin-and-alcohol) guides go deeper. Excedrin is worth flagging because it contains aspirin *and* acetaminophen *and* caffeine, so it carries both the stomach risk and the liver risk.

**Don't double up.** Taking ibuprofen and naproxen together, or adding aspirin on top of either, doesn't give you better relief. It adds to the stomach and kidney load. One NSAID at a time.

## Prescription NSAIDs and Alcohol

Prescription NSAIDs have the same core interaction with alcohol. Many of them are stronger per dose, and people often take them every day for weeks or months for arthritis or chronic pain. That steady daily use is what changes the risk, because the stomach and kidneys never get a break.

**Meloxicam (Mobic)** is one of the most prescribed NSAIDs in the US. It has a long half-life (roughly 15 to 20 hours) and is taken once a day, so there's no point in the day when it isn't in your system. Our [meloxicam and alcohol](/never-hungover/meloxicam-and-alcohol) guide covers it in depth.

**Diclofenac** tablets are a strong NSAID and, as mentioned above, the one most often linked to rare liver injury. Some versions (Arthrotec) are combined with misoprostol, a drug that protects the stomach. Diclofenac **gel** (Voltaren Arthritis Pain, sold over the counter in the US since 2020) is applied to the skin, and much less of it reaches the bloodstream than with tablets, so the stomach and kidney concerns are much smaller. It's still worth following the label.

**Celecoxib (Celebrex)** mainly blocks COX-2 rather than COX-1. Because COX-1 is the one that protects the stomach, celecoxib tends to be gentler on the stomach than older NSAIDs. Gentler is not the same as safe. It still carries a stomach bleeding warning, it still affects the kidneys, and alcohol still irritates the stomach on its own.

**Ketorolac** (formerly sold as Toradol) is one of the most potent NSAIDs and is only meant for a few days of use, usually after surgery or an injury. It has boxed warnings about stomach bleeding and kidney problems. Drinking while on a ketorolac course is a poor idea, and you should ask your prescriber before having any alcohol.

**All prescription NSAIDs (and OTC ones other than aspirin) carry an FDA warning about heart attack and stroke risk.** The FDA strengthened that warning in 2015. The risk is higher at higher doses and with longer use. Heavy drinking raises blood pressure on its own, so the two can add up for people who already have heart disease or high blood pressure.

If you take a prescription NSAID every day, the most useful thing you can do is ask your doctor or pharmacist one simple question: "How much alcohol is reasonable for me on this?" The answer depends on your dose, your age, your stomach history, and your other medicines, and they can also tell you whether you should be taking a stomach-protecting medicine alongside it.

## Can You Drink While Taking NSAIDs?

For an occasional drink, the honest answer for most healthy adults is that a drink or two while taking an NSAID at the label dose, with food, is unlikely to cause a serious problem. The label warning is aimed at people who have **3 or more drinks every day**, and the bleeding risk climbs with both the amount of alcohol and the amount of NSAID.

That doesn't mean it's risk-free. The chance of stomach irritation and bleeding is higher than with either alone, and you won't know you're the unlucky one until symptoms show up. The risk is clearly higher if you:

- Drink heavily or binge, rather than having one or two drinks
- Take the NSAID on an empty stomach
- Take more than the label dose, or take it for many days in a row
- Are over 60
- Have had a stomach ulcer or bleeding before
- Also take a blood thinner, a steroid like prednisone, or an SSRI antidepressant (all of which raise bleeding risk)
- Have kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure
- Also take blood pressure medicines called ACE inhibitors or ARBs plus a diuretic ("water pill"). Doctors call NSAIDs plus those two the "triple whammy" for the kidneys, and alcohol-related dehydration makes it worse.

If any of those apply to you, it's worth checking with a pharmacist before mixing the two at all.

## How Long After Taking an NSAID Can You Drink (and Vice Versa)?

There is no official waiting period that applies to everyone, and anyone who gives you an exact number of hours that fits all people is guessing. What you can reason from is how long each drug lasts.

- **Ibuprofen** mostly clears within a day, and its effects fade much sooner. Waiting several hours after a dose before drinking, and not taking another dose while you're drinking, is a sensible approach for a healthy adult.
- **Naproxen** lasts much longer. A single dose is still active 12 hours later, so if you took Aleve in the morning, it will likely still be in your system that evening.
- **Aspirin's** effect on clotting lasts about a week after a dose, even though the drug itself clears quickly.
- **Once-a-day prescription NSAIDs** like meloxicam are always in your system. There's no "gap" to drink in, so this is a question for your prescriber.

Going the other way, if you've been drinking and want a painkiller, the better move is to wait until the alcohol has cleared. Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot between people. After a heavy night, that can take well into the next day. Drink water and eat something before you take the NSAID.

## Should You Take an NSAID for a Hangover?

You *can*, and for a hangover headache an NSAID is often a reasonable choice for a healthy adult who doesn't drink heavily day to day. Some researchers think part of the hangover is driven by inflammation, which is one reason NSAIDs get mentioned. But be realistic about what they do and don't do.

**What an NSAID can help with:** the headache, and general aches.

**What it won't fix:** nausea, dehydration, poor sleep, low blood sugar, anxiety, or the general washed-out feeling. There is no good evidence that NSAIDs shorten a hangover or treat its causes.

**Why the morning after is a delicate time:** your stomach is already irritated, you're probably dehydrated, and you may not have eaten. Those are the exact conditions that make NSAIDs harder on the stomach and kidneys.

If you do take one for a hangover:

1. **Drink a full glass of water first**, and keep drinking through the morning.
2. **Eat something.** Even toast or crackers helps protect the stomach.
3. **Take one standard dose.** More won't help your headache more.
4. **Don't take it if you've been vomiting a lot** or can't keep fluids down. That's the most dehydrated state, and the kidneys are most vulnerable. Rehydrate first.
5. **Pick one painkiller.** Don't take ibuprofen and then add Aleve two hours later because the first one didn't work fast enough.

### Never take an NSAID "pre-emptively"

A common habit is to take ibuprofen or aspirin before bed after drinking, in the hope of avoiding a morning headache. Don't. You'd be adding an NSAID while the alcohol is still in your stomach and bloodstream, usually on an empty stomach, often while dehydrated, and before you even know you'll need it. If you wake up with a headache, deal with it then, after water and food. For habits that actually make a difference, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## NSAIDs vs Acetaminophen After Drinking: Which Is Safer?

Neither is risk-free. They put different organs at risk.

| | NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin) | Acetaminophen (Tylenol) |
|---|---|---|
| Main organ at risk with alcohol | Stomach and kidneys | Liver |
| Label alcohol warning | Stomach bleeding with 3+ drinks a day | Liver damage with 3+ drinks a day |
| Worst time to take it | Empty stomach, dehydrated, or with a blood thinner | Regular heavy drinker, fasting, or extra doses from combination products |
| Reduces inflammation | Yes | Not in the same way |

A rough way to think about it: if you have a history of stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or take a blood thinner, acetaminophen may be the better fit, as long as you don't drink heavily on a regular basis. If you drink heavily day to day or have liver disease, acetaminophen needs much more caution, and an NSAID isn't automatically safe either. People with liver disease are sometimes told to use low-dose acetaminophen rather than an NSAID. This is exactly the kind of choice a pharmacist can make in two minutes with your medication list in front of them.

One more rule: don't take an NSAID and acetaminophen together the morning after "for extra strength" unless a doctor has told you to. Some combination products do this on purpose at fixed doses, but stacking separate pills makes it easy to lose count.

## Warning Signs: When to See a Doctor

Most people who take a single NSAID dose after drinking have no problems. But stomach bleeding can come on without much warning, and kidney problems can be quiet at first. These are the signs to watch for.

**Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US) if you notice:**

- Vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
- Black, sticky, tar-like stools, or blood in your stool
- Severe or sudden stomach pain that doesn't go away
- Feeling faint, dizzy, very weak, or short of breath, or a racing heart along with any of the above
- Chest pain, weakness on one side of the body, or slurred speech

**See a doctor soon if you notice:**

- Ongoing stomach pain, burning, or indigestion that keeps coming back after drinking and taking painkillers
- Urinating much less than normal, or very dark urine even after rehydrating
- New swelling in your ankles, feet, or legs
- Nausea and vomiting that keep you from holding down fluids for more than a day
- Unusual bruising or bleeding

If someone has taken far more than the label dose of any NSAID, especially together with a lot of alcohol, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) for advice, even if they seem fine.

## Safer Habits If You Use NSAIDs and Drink

These won't make the combination risk-free, but they cut the risk meaningfully:

- **Use the lowest dose that works, for the shortest time.** That's the standard advice for every NSAID, with or without alcohol.
- **Always take NSAIDs with food and a full glass of water.**
- **Keep drinks moderate and spaced out.** Alternate alcoholic drinks with water.
- **Don't take NSAIDs to "pre-treat" a hangover.**
- **Read every label.** Check cold, flu, sinus, and sleep products for a second NSAID or for acetaminophen.
- **Consider a topical NSAID for joint or muscle pain.** A gel on the skin puts far less of the drug into your bloodstream than a tablet.
- **If you take a daily prescription NSAID, ask about stomach protection.** Doctors sometimes prescribe an acid-reducing medicine alongside it for people at higher risk.
- **Tell your pharmacist how much you drink.** They aren't judging you. They need it to give you the right advice.

For a wider look at how common medicines and supplements interact, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## A Better Path Than Painkillers the Morning After

If you're reading about NSAIDs and alcohol because you regularly wake up needing a painkiller, the painkiller isn't really the problem to solve. The most effective steps are the plain ones: drink less, drink more slowly, eat before and while you drink, and alternate alcohol with water.

Some people also add supplements. Here's an honest view of one we cover a lot:

- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. It's promising, not proven. There is no good evidence that DHM protects your stomach or kidneys from NSAIDs, and it does not make it safe to combine an NSAID with heavy drinking. If you want to try it as part of a broader approach, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medicines, check with your pharmacist before adding any supplement.

No supplement should change how you use an NSAID. Follow the label, take it with food and water, and respect the alcohol warning whatever else you take.

## The Bottom Line

- NSAIDs include ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin, plus prescription drugs like meloxicam, diclofenac, and celecoxib. They all share the same basic interaction with alcohol.
- The main risks are **stomach bleeding, kidney strain when you're dehydrated, and slower blood clotting**. The liver is less of a concern than with acetaminophen.
- One standard dose with food and water the morning after a few drinks is unlikely to harm a healthy adult. Risk climbs with heavy or daily drinking, higher doses, empty stomachs, dehydration, age over 60, and other medicines like blood thinners.
- Naproxen and once-daily prescription NSAIDs last much longer than ibuprofen, and aspirin's clotting effect lasts about a week.
- Don't take an NSAID before bed to prevent a hangover, and don't stack two NSAIDs.
- Vomiting blood, black stools, severe stomach pain, or feeling faint are emergencies.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking NSAIDs?**

For most healthy adults, a drink or two while taking an over-the-counter NSAID at the label dose, with food, is unlikely to cause serious harm. But the combination raises the risk of stomach irritation and bleeding, and the risk goes up with heavier drinking, higher doses, and longer use. US labels warn that stomach bleeding is more likely if you have 3 or more drinks a day. If you drink that much, are over 60, have had ulcers, or take a blood thinner, ask a doctor or pharmacist first.

**Which NSAID is safest with alcohol?**

None is risk-free, because they all reduce the prostaglandins that protect your stomach and kidneys. Ibuprofen is the shortest-acting, so its effects overlap less with drinking later in the day. Naproxen lasts much longer, and aspirin affects blood clotting for about a week. Celecoxib (prescription) tends to be gentler on the stomach but still carries a bleeding warning. A topical NSAID gel puts much less drug into your bloodstream than a tablet.

**How long after taking ibuprofen or naproxen can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone. Ibuprofen's effects fade within several hours, so waiting a few hours after a dose and not taking another while drinking is a sensible approach for a healthy adult. Naproxen is still active 12 hours or more after a dose, so it will usually overlap with drinking the same day. If you take a once-daily prescription NSAID like meloxicam, ask your prescriber what's reasonable.

**Is it OK to take an NSAID for a hangover?**

For a healthy adult who doesn't drink heavily day to day, one standard dose for a hangover headache, taken with food and water, is usually reasonable. It only helps with pain, though. There's no good evidence that NSAIDs fix dehydration, nausea, or the other causes of a hangover. Skip it if you've been vomiting a lot or can't keep fluids down, since that's when your kidneys are most vulnerable.

**Is it safe to take ibuprofen or aspirin before bed after drinking to prevent a hangover?**

No. Taking an NSAID while alcohol is still in your system, usually on an empty stomach and while dehydrated, adds to the strain on your stomach and kidneys, and there's no good evidence that it prevents a hangover. If you wake up with a headache, drink water, eat something, and then take a single dose if you still need it.

**Are NSAIDs or Tylenol better after drinking?**

They carry different risks. NSAIDs mainly put the stomach and kidneys at risk, while acetaminophen (Tylenol) mainly puts the liver at risk. If you have a history of ulcers or kidney problems or take a blood thinner, acetaminophen may fit better, as long as you don't drink heavily on a regular basis. If you drink heavily most days or have liver disease, talk to a doctor before using either.

**What are the signs of stomach bleeding from NSAIDs and alcohol?**

Watch for vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds, black or tar-like stools, severe stomach pain, or feeling faint, dizzy, or weak. Any of these needs emergency care right away. Ongoing stomach burning or pain that keeps coming back after drinking and taking painkillers is also worth seeing a doctor about.

**Can I drink while taking a prescription NSAID like meloxicam or Celebrex?**

Ask your prescriber, because the answer depends on your dose, age, stomach history, and other medicines. Prescription NSAIDs are often taken every day, so they're always in your system and there's no safe "gap" to drink in. Occasional light drinking may be acceptable for some people, while others will be told to avoid alcohol or to take a stomach-protecting medicine alongside the NSAID.
